newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB says wheat sales not distorting U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: CWB says wheat sales not distorting U.S. market.

text.p: Canadian wheat and durum sales to processors in the United States are not distorting the U.S. wheat market, Canadian Wheat Board chief commissioner Lorne Hehn said Tuesday.
"We sell in there at fully competitive values so there's no trade distorting going on," Hehn said in an interview.

Earlier on Tuesday U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told the U.S. House Agriculture Committee that he was monitoring Canadian wheat exports, which sparked a bitter bilateral trade dispute three years ago.
"We are monitoring it. We will not tolerate market disruptions from imports of Canadian grain," Glickman said.

Hehn said the CWB has been routing some wheat and barley exports through the United States to Pacific Northwest and Gulf ports since early January because of weather and equipment-related delays in delivering grain to Vancouver.

"When I first heard about this I thought he was referring to 100,000 or so tonnes we're moving through the United States for export, but obviously he's zeroed in on our exports into the domestic processors in the U.S.," Hehn said.
Hehn said those exports for U.S. consumption were fully in line with past agreements and trade rules.

A bilateral agreement to cap Canadian wheat and durum sales to the U.S. at 1.5 million tonnes a year expired on September 12, 1995, and cannot be reimposed under world trade rules, according to Agriculture Canada.

According to Canadian Grain Commission figures, Canada sold 608,300 tonnes of milling wheat to the U.S. from August 1, 1996, to January 31, 1997, compared to 375,600 tonnes in the same period a year earlier.
Canada also sold 152,300 tonnes of durum to the U.S. from August 1 to January 31, against 72,000 tonnes in the same period a year earlier.
